Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Expectation2: Contribute to community well-being through paying taxes, following public health and safety guidance, and helping in emergencies
Situation2: A flash-flood warning triggers building alarms as water rises along the block.
Story: My phone buzzed violently just as the emergency sirens outside began to wail. I glanced at the screen—my friend’s name flashed, and when I answered, her voice was shaky. Her car had broken down on the highway, miles away, and she was stranded, scared, and desperate for help. She begged me to come get her right away. At the same moment, the city’s flood alert blared through my apartment, and I could see water creeping up the street from my window. The authorities had warned everyone to stay indoors, avoid travel, and prepare for possible evacuation. As a citizen, I knew I was expected to follow these safety protocols, not only for my own good but to avoid putting emergency responders at risk. But as a friend, I felt the pull to rush out and rescue her, to be there when she needed me most. My heart pounded as I stared at my keys, torn between loyalty to my friend and my responsibility to my community.
